title: Mark Python-2.0.1, PSF-2.0, CNRI-Python-GPL-Compatible and CNRI-Python as FSF Free/Libre
body:
The FSF page on licensing covers the different Python licenses.

Both [License of Python 1.6a2 and earlier versions](https://directory.fsf.org/wiki?title=License:Python1.6a2) and [License of Python 2.0.1, 2.1.1, and newer versions](https://directory.fsf.org/wiki?title=License:Python2.0.1) are included in the list of licenses that "qualify as free software licenses, and are compatible with the GNU GPL".
The [License of Python 1.6b1 through 2.0 and 2.1](https://directory.fsf.org/wiki/License:Python1.6b1) is included in the list of licenses that "are free software licenses, but are not compatible with the GNU GPL.

[FSF's entry for Python 2.0.1, 2.1.1](https://directory.fsf.org/wiki/License:Python-2.0.1) identically matches text of `Python-2.0.1` and contains the following licenses with separate SPDX-identifiers: `PSF-2.0`, `CNRI-Python-GPL-Compatible`.

I conclude that `Python-2.0.1`, `PSF-2.0` and `CNRI-Python-GPL-Compatible` are GPL-compatible Free Software licenses.

[FSF's entry for Python 1.6.b1](https://directory.fsf.org/wiki/License:Python-1.6b1) closely matches the text of `CNRI-Python`. It is not exactly the same as FSF lists the license of Python 1.6 (non-beta) and SPDX entry for `NCRI-Python` contains the 1.6-beta-1 version. The key distinction with `CNRI-Python-GPL-Compatible` is article 7 that specifies applicable law. Article 7 is equal between FSF's entry for Python 1.6.b1 and `CNRI-Python`.

I conclude that `CNRI-Python` is a Free Software license that is not GPL-compatible, but it should still get the 'y' in the 'FSF Free/Libre' column.

For completeness, the `Python-2.0` license is already marked OSI-approved and Free Software and contains the license texts of `PSF-2.0` and `CNRI-Python-GPL-Compatible`.

I was triggered to submit this issue by [discussions for choosing the appropriate license identifier for the Argparse NPM package](https://github.com/nodeca/argparse/pull/188).

I couldn't figure out the source of the 'FSF Free/Libre'-column. Perhaps it can be improved in the documentation.

body:
### How license meets inclusion principles

The Space Child License is a permissive licence carrying a use restriction (a "Peace Clause"). It grants broad, royalty-free rights for peaceful use and withdraws them for seven enumerated harms: armed aggression, civilian-targeting weapons systems, autonomous lethal decision-making, mass surveillance for persecution, suppression of expression and assembly, severe environmental destruction, and forced labour or trafficking.

**Against the definitive factors**

**A. Does not match an existing entry.** Nothing currently on the list pairs a permissive grant with this clause set. The nearest relatives are `Hippocratic-2.1` and `Hippocratic-3.0-core`, and the difference is structural rather than cosmetic: those incorporate external human-rights standards wholesale, whereas this licence enumerates specific prohibited uses inline and then, in section 8.6, names the instruments those terms are to be read against.

**B. Not OSI-approved, and not submitted to OSI.** Stated plainly rather than left to be discovered: a field-of-use restriction is incompatible with OSD §6 and with FSF freedom 0, so this licence is not open source under either definition and is not presented as one. The project README says so in those words, so that nobody adopts it expecting otherwise.

**C. Applies to source code, not only executables.** Section 3 conditions redistribution on retaining notices and does not restrict source availability.

**D. The text is identifiable and stable.** v1.0 is final and not in drafting. It is byte-identical across all 37 adopting repositories — 14,714 bytes, `sha256 bb4b0941a67dcd6c…` — verified by hashing the file independently in five of them before writing this.

**E. Versioning commitment.** The steward commits to not modifying the v1.0 text after addition to the list. Any future change will ship as a new version with its own number and its own file. This is published as policy in the canonical repository rather than only asserted here.

**Against the other factors**

**1 / 4.** The licence does not meet an OSI or FSF definition, so factor 4 is the applicable route: it is primarily intended for the free distribution of source code with limited restrictions. The restrictions are a closed list of seven, each tied to an existing international instrument rather than to the licensor's discretion, and they bind *conduct* rather than field of commerce — commercial use, modification, redistribution and private use are all unconditionally permitted.

**2. Structured to be generally usable by anyone.** The operative text contains no reference to any project, product, organization or person. A single attribution line in the closing footer names the authors; it imposes no obligation and does not scope the grant. Any third party can adopt the text unchanged.

**3. Actual use.** 37 repositories, 24 of them public, spanning an industrial-control platform, an operating-system kernel, a Rust agent runtime and the libraries beneath them.

Stated candidly, because it is the weakest point of this submission: **that use is concentrated in a single organization.** The licence has not yet been adopted outside `kannaka-labs`. We are submitting now precisely because the absence of an identifier is what blocks wider adoption — registries and scanners resolve it as `NOASSERTION` and deny by default, which is operationally identical to carrying no licence at all. We would rather have that weighed openly than found.

**5.** The steward is the submitter and supports this submission.

If the Legal Team concludes that adoption is currently too narrow, we would welcome that answer stated as such, so we can return when the evidence is stronger rather than re-litigate it now.

A variant of the `Xerox` license was used for Tiny CLOS, a Scheme version of the Common Lisp Object System. In addition to Tiny CLOS itself, the license applies to derived software, like Racket's Swindle and Guile's GOOPS.

This pull request attempts to add markup to the `Xerox` license to support matching the Tiny CLOS variant: I've written it in the form of a pull request to be concrete, but I'm not very familiar with the markup schema—corrections and improvements are very welcome!

The text from the header of `tiny-clos.scm` in  https://www.cs.cmu.edu/afs/cs/project/ai-repository/ai/lang/scheme/oop/tinyclos/tinyclos.tgz is:

```scheme
; **********************************************************************

; above copyright notice of Xerox Corporation, this paragraph and the

```
(Alternatively, the copy from Swindle is [on GitHub](https://github.com/racket/swindle/blob/122e38efb9842394ef6462053991efb4bd0edf3b/tiny-clos.rkt#L14-L31).)

The only differences from the current text of the `Xerox` license are the year in the copyright text—which IIUC is ignored for matching anyway—and the simplified first sentence. title: New License: MIT-PoU
body:
Requests the addition of the **MIT License with Proof-of-Usage Condition (MIT-PoU)** to the SPDX License List. Closes #3068, which carries the full inclusion-principles analysis; the short version:

The MIT grant, word for word, plus one condition addressed to operators of automated systems, in two halves: record the usage in the repository's register (`PROOF_OF_USAGE.md`, one row via pull request), and credit the work in whatever the usage produced, alongside a SHA-256 provenance hash — `SHA-256("System:Operator:ISODate:RepoURL")` — so either half can be checked against the other by anyone, with no central registry.

- **Text:** frozen at [tag v1.2.0](https://github.com/origami-ltd/mit-proof-of-usage-license/blob/v1.2.0/LICENSE.md); the steward commits that the text at that tag does not change after addition, and that any change to the terms is a new version under a new identifier.
- **Not OSI open source, and not claimed to be** — the added obligation makes it source-available; stated in the licence's own documentation, which also flags the credits half's BSD-4-Clause-style GPL incompatibility rather than leaving it to be discovered.
- **In use by seven repositories, three not the steward's:** [mrxenginner/reVC](https://github.com/mrxenginner/reVC) (~257★, previously unlicensed by its authors' explicit note; adopted 13 Aug 2026 in [reVC#37](https://github.com/mrxenginner/reVC/pull/37)), [Polyphase-Labs/Polyphase-Engine](https://github.com/Polyphase-Labs/Polyphase-Engine) (~55★, a previously unlicensed game engine; adopted 16 Aug 2026 in [#50](https://github.com/Polyphase-Labs/Polyphase-Engine/pull/50), merged by the project's own maintainer account, with its own copyright holder in the notice and both the register and the discovery document present), and [gumiranda/cloudfunding](https://github.com/gumiranda/cloudfunding) (14 Aug 2026; its copyright notice names its author and the steward jointly — stated here rather than found). The other four: [wasm.com.br](https://github.com/origami-ltd/wasm.com.br), [wasm-generals](https://github.com/origami-ltd/wasm-generals) (`web/` portion; the engine is GPL-3.0 and deliberately carries none of this), [wasm-revc](https://github.com/origami-ltd/wasm-revc), and [the licence's own repository](https://github.com/origami-ltd/mit-proof-of-usage-license). All three outside adoptions were proposed by the steward as pull requests and merged by their own maintainers.

**Files:**
- `src/MIT-PoU.xml` — marked up per `DOCS/xml-fields.md`: copyright as the standard replaceable field, the register filename under an `alt` tag since the text itself calls it a suggestion.
- `test/simpleTestForGenerator/MIT-PoU.txt` — the canonical text, UTF-8, ASCII-clean.

Steward: Erasmo Bellumat / Origami 限. Happy to adjust markup or metadata to whatever the Legal Team prefers.

title: Consider differentiating customizable text from simple variation-handling?
body: ## Uses of `` Currently, the `` tag is used in two fundamentally different capacities. ### As a field to mark customizable text Many of the license texts include customizable details related to the project being licensed, like project name, copyright statements, maintainer or rightsholder addresses, etc. These are frequently wrapped in an alt tag that will match anything (`match=".*"`), although a few have more specific matching patterns. A variable name is always specified (name="something") to capture the matched string. For example, in `BSD-2-Clause.xml`, the text specifying "THE COPYRIGHT HOLDER(S) (AND|OR) CONTRIBUTORS" are made customizable in two places, captured as `copyrightHolderAsIs` and `copyrightHolderLiability`: https://github.com/spdx/license-list-XML/blob/9269d7211fba83092697d5211c5f81988222ec84/src/BSD-2-Clause.xml#L30 https://github.com/spdx/license-list-XML/blob/9269d7211fba83092697d5211c5f81988222ec84/src/BSD-2-Clause.xml#L33 In `Python-2.0.1.xml`, the specific Python version for which the license applies is similarly captured in a number of places, using a more specific regular expression: https://github.com/spdx/license-list-XML/blob/9269d7211fba83092697d5211c5f81988222ec84/src/Python-2.0.1.xml#L35 https://github.com/spdx/license-list-XML/blob/9269d7211fba83092697d5211c5f81988222ec84/src/Python-2.0.1.xml#L84 ### To support minor variations in license texts Other uses of alt tags aren't free-form/customizable at all, but merely prevent slight variations in license text from causing a failure to match the license. Going back to `BSD-2-Clause.xml`, the word "EXPRESS" is surrounded by an alt tag not because it's customizable, but simply because some versions of the text contain "EXPRESSED" instead of "EXPRESS": https://github.com/spdx/license-list-XML/blob/9269d7211fba83092697d5211c5f81988222ec84/src/BSD-2-Clause.xml#L31 The same is true in `xpp.xml`, where "University" may be misspelled as "Univeristy", and where a certain conjunction may be either "and" or "or" (but nothing else): https://github.com/spdx/license-list-XML/blob/9269d7211fba83092697d5211c5f81988222ec84/src/xpp.xml#L40 ### Other tags handled as replaceable This also applies to e.g. `` and ``, which are presented identically as red replaceable text, despite having different purposes. It makes sense for a project to customize the copyright text of its license as needed, so `` can fairly be treated like the first category of `` tags above. But the bullets used in the license are more akin to the second type of `` tag above, in that there are a fairly limited set of possibilities for what might be found in their place. The `1.` before the first clause in `BSD-2-Clause.xml` might be replaced with `1)`, or `1 —`, or even nothing if the list is numbered automatically, but it probably shouldn't be replaced with `45)` or `apple)`. ## Presentation of `` Software doesn't care about the purpose of a given `` tag, and for the purposes of matching the information that it's replaceable is sufficient. But to humans, the implications of the two types of "replaceable" text are unlikely to be the same. And because these two very different situations are _handled_ the same way in the code/data, they're also **presented** the same way on the website. All replaceable text is presented in red, so the handling of variations appears to indicate that unexpected bits of text are customizable or free-form, when in fact they're not. In the display of `BSD-2-Clause.xml`, for example, it seems potentially confusing for "EXPRESS" to be shown in the same red text as "THE COPYRIGHT HOLDERS AND CONTRIBUTORS" — at least, without also providing some explanation for why and how someone would "customize" the word EXPRESS: ![image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/552e8ce1-7600-4867-8f2b-3f9f757a9c98) Since optional and replaceable texts _are_ indicated to humans by coloring the text blue or red, respectively, it's presumably of some value to highlight those locations. But if "there could be anything here" freely-customizable areas of the text, and other areas where only a very limited set of options will pass, are all presented the same, it seems as though that value could be somewhat reduced?

**1.** License name: Archive Packaging Exception
**2.** Short identifier: Archive-packaging-exception
**3.** License author or steward: ale5000
**4.** Comments: This exception addresses a specific gap in the current SPDX License List regarding the distribution of software in aggregated, compressed, or containerized formats.
While existing exceptions focus on software linking (API/Library), this proposal focuses on the Packaging Process.

Possible uses:

1) System and Platform Modding: In ecosystems such as mobile platforms, custom firmware, and embedded systems, GPLv3-licensed automation scripts must be bundled into installable archives (e.g., flashable ZIPs).
These archives often require the inclusion of independent third-party modules or assets with incompatible licenses. This exception provides a clear legal framework to treat these as "Independent Modules" within the same distribution container.

2) Containerization (Docker and OCI Images): As software moves toward containerized distribution, users often build images where GPLv3 components coexist with proprietary or differently licensed tools.
This exception clarifies that such bundling—where components interact through standard interfaces—does not extend the copyleft requirements to the entire container image.

3) Modern CI/CD and Security Compliance: Modern distribution requires archives to be validated and digitally signed.
This exception explicitly protects the use of digital signing tools, code coverage, and profiling analysis tools within an "Eligible Packaging Process," ensuring that security and quality compliance do not conflict with the license terms.

4) Protection of Copyleft Integrity: A key feature of this exception is the explicit exclusion of derivative works.
It ensures that "Independent Modules" must be truly independent under copyright law. If a module is based on the GPLv3 components, it remains subject to the full GPLv3 requirements, thus preventing any "weakening" of the core copyleft protections.

title: Consider changes to Unicode-TOU

body:
This is following from the discussion on the spdx-legal mailing list at https://lists.spdx.org/g/Spdx-legal/topic/97116566

[`Unicode-TOU`](https://spdx.org/licenses/Unicode-TOU.html) is not a versioned identifier. It points to the license text for the Unicode Terms of Use as they existed as of (I believe) 2014. But the terms of use posted on the Unicode website at https://www.unicode.org/copyright.html have evolved over time, and the mailing list thread discusses how this has caused some confusion with folks using `Unicode-TOU` to refer to the wrong set of terms.

A separate issue #1851 discusses whether to add a new, separate identifier with the current updated terms.

For the current `Unicode-TOU` identifier, we should consider either or both of the following options:
1. For the license's `Full name`, modify it to be `Unicode Terms of Use - 2014` or something similar, to help emphasize that it is the 2014 version (again, assuming that's the correct year - should be verified); and/or
2. Deprecate `Unicode-TOU` as an identifier, and add a new ID `Unicode-TOU-2014` with the same existing content.

I'm in favor of 1, and on the fence for 2. Interested in other community members' thoughts.

For clarity, in neither case would we remove `Unicode-TOU` as a valid identifier. It would remain valid (even if deprecated) and pointing to the existing license text that's currently associated with it.

title: SimPL-2.0: Fix OSI URL and mark last section as optional
body:
The last section of SimPL-2.0 text is not strictly part of the license itself, so this PR marks it as optional, to avoid conveying misleading guidance to users.

Additionally, the OSI URL (modified in PR #2960) has incorrect capitalization: it is written as "SiMPL" instead of "SimPL". Although that URL does work, resolving to the correct page, the capitalization does not match the actual license's short name, and can be potentially misleading, so this PR also corrects the URL.

While modifying the file, I took the opportunity to fix some indentation inconsistencies in this file.

Finally, this PR corrects a punctuation inconsistency in the list of disclaimers: the last item in that list currently ends with a semicolon, which is a leftover from an [earlier draft](https://lists.opensource.org/pipermail/license-discuss_lists.opensource.org/2007-March/012630.html) in which an additional list item followed it. When that extra item was removed, the semicolon in the item before it should have been adjusted to a period, but that detail appears to have been missed at the time. This PR fixes the punctuation to ensure the consistency of the recorded text.

Each of the changes above are made in separate, atomic commits, so that they can be reviewed independently (I would suggest viewing the [diff in whitespace-insensitive mode](https://github.com/spdx/license-list-XML/pull/2988/changes?w=1)), and dropped if undesirable (or split to separate PRs if that's preferred).
